title: Comparison and logical operators
learningGoals: combine tests with and, or and not
print bool values as true and false

youtube.title: C++ Comparison and Logical Operators | C++ Programming EP 08
youtube.description: In this episode you will compare two values, combine tests with and, or and not and print bool values as true and false, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Comparison and logical operators · 0:54 Four questions · 1:34 Truth table · 2:04 Second program · 3:04 Recap · 3:35 Bug of the Day · 4:23 Challenge · 4:43 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "TRUE OR FALSE" in tomato on pastel blue; Xecxec next to a traffic light with a green tick and a red cross; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a traffic light with a green tick and a red cross

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we ask questions in code. Is a number bigger? Are two values equal? Each answer is true or false.

scenes.onScreen: "Comparison and logical operators": numbered lines (1. A comparison gives true or false; 2. And needs both tests true; 3. Or needs one test true) and an analogy card: a cinema gate: you need a ticket and the right age
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A comparison asks a question about two values. The answer is a bool, so it is true or false. The comparison operators are less than, greater than, equal to and not equal to. The logical operators join tests. And needs both tests to be true. Or needs only one. Not flips the answer. Think of a cinema gate. You need a ticket and the right age.
points: A comparison gives true or false

analogy.title: Comparison and logical operators
analogy.body: A cinema gate: you need a ticket and the right age

scenes.onScreen: logic.cpp: four tests print true or false
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 7] Boolalpha makes cout print true and false instead of one and zero. [HL 8] Is seventeen greater than or equal to eighteen? No, so false. [HL 9] Is age under eighteen, and does the person have a pass? Both are true, so the answer is true. [HL 10] Is age seventeen, or is it eighteen? One test is true, so the answer is true. [HL 11] Not has pass flips true into false.

scenes.onScreen: a table for and, or and not
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: This table shows all cases for two tests, A and B. And is true only in the first row. Or is false only in the last row. Not has one input. It always gives the opposite value.

diagram.caption: a table for and, or and not

scenes.onScreen: range.cpp: is a mark between zero and one hundred?
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The mark is seventy-two. [HL 6] A valid mark must be at least zero and at most one hundred. We join two tests with and. [HL 7] A pass needs at least thirty-five. [HL 8] Both bools print as true. Always write the two tests in full. Never write zero less than mark less than one hundred.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as range dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints true and true.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A comparison gives a bool. Two. Use two equals signs to test for equality. Three. And needs both tests true, or needs one, and not flips the answer. Four. Boolalpha prints true and false as words. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Use two equals signs to test for equality.
And needs both tests true, or needs one, and not flips the answer.
Boolalpha prints true and false as words.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: One equals sign instead of two
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Here the if test uses one equals sign. That does not compare. It stores zero in seats. The compiler warns about an assignment used as a truth value. Use two equals signs to compare. Always read warnings. They often point at real bugs.

scenes.onScreen: Why was the boolean so honest? It only knew true or false.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why was the boolean so honest? It only knew true or false.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: test whether a year is a leap year
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write one bool expression that is true when a number is even and bigger than ten. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 09 · Type conversion and casting
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: type conversion and casting. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

check.cpp: In function 'int main()':
check.cpp:6:15: warning: suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value [-Wparentheses]
    6 |     if (seats = 0) {
      |         ~~~~~~^~~
bug.why: A single equals sign stores a value. Two equals signs compare. The wrong test also changes seats to zero.

pun: "Why was the boolean so honest? It only knew true or false."
challenge: Write one bool expression that is true when a number is even and bigger than ten.
challengeAnswer: Use n remainder two equals equals zero, and n greater than ten, joined with two ampersands.
